la:adj:popularis.gloss: popular (by, of or for the people)
senses: popular (by, of or for the people)
of the same people or country

dedicated or belonging to the people, as opposed to the nobility
la:adj:popularis.html:
pŏpŭlāris (sync. poplāris, ), e, adj.
1. populus
,
of or belonging to the people, proceeding from or designed for the people.
In gen.: populares leges,i. e. laws instituted by the people,: accessus,: coetus,: munus,a donation to the people,: popularia verba usitata,; cf.: ad usum popularem atque civilem disserere,: dictio ad vulgarem popularemque sensum accommodata,: oratio philosophorum ... nec sententiis nec verbis instructa popularibus,: popularis oratio,: populari nomine aliquid appellare,: laudes,in the mouths of the people,: admiratio,: honor,: ventus,popular favor,: aura,: civitas,democracy, (opp. regia civitas, monarchy): popularia sacra sunt, ut ait Labeo, quae omnes cives faciunt nec certis familiis attributa sunt, Müll.—
Subst.: pŏpŭlārĭa, ĭum, n. (sc. subsellia), the seats of the people in the theatre, the common seats, ; —
In partic.
Of or belonging to the same people or country, native, indigenous (as an adj. rare): Sappho puellis de popularibus querentem vidimus,: flumina,of the same district,: oliva,native,.—
As subst.: pŏpŭlāris, is, comm. (freq. and class.).
Masc., a countryman, fellow-countryman: redire ad suos populares, Naev. ap. Fest. s. v. stuprum, p. 317 Müll.: o mi popularis, salve,: o populares,; : popularis ac sodalis suus,: ego vero Solonis, popularis tui, ut puto, etiam mei, legem neglegam (for Cicero had also lived in Athens),: popularis alicujus definiti loci (opp. civis totius mundi),: non populares modo,: cum turbā popularium,: quae res indicabat populares esse.—
Fem.: mea popularis opsecro haec est?; ; ; : tibi popularis,.—
Transf.
Of animals and plants of the same region: leaena, Ov. lb. 503: (glires) populares ejusdem silvae (opp. alienigenae, amne vel monte discreti),: populares eorum (prunorum) myxae,.—
Of persons of the same condition, occupation, tastes, etc., a companion, partner, associate, accomplice, comrade: meus popularis Geta, fellow (i. e. a slave), : populares conjurationis,; : sceleris,: invitis hoc nostris popularibus dicam, the men of our school, i. e. the Stoics, .—
In a political signification, of or belonging to the people, attached or devoted to the people (as opposed to the nobility), popular, democratic: res publica ex tribus generibus illis, regali et optumati et populari confusa modice, (ap. ): homo maxime popularis,: consul veritate non ostentatione popularis,: animus vere popularis, saluti populi consulens, : ingenium,: sacerdos, i. e. Clodius, as attached to the popular party,: vir,: homo, of the common people (opp. rex), . —Hence, subst.: pŏpŭlāres, ĭum, m., the people's party, the democrats (opp. optimates, the aristocrats): duo genera semper in hac civitate fuerunt . . . quibus ex generibus alteri se populares, alteri optimates et haberi et esse voluerunt. Quia ea quae faciebant, multitudini jucunda esse volebant, populares habebantur,: qui populares habebantur,: ex quo evenit, ut alii populares, alii studiosi optimi cujusque videantur,.—
Acceptable to the people, agreeable to the multitude, popular: dixi in senatu me popularem consulem futurum. Quid enim est tam populare quam pax?: potest nihil esse tam populare quam id quod ego consul popularis adfero, pacem, etc.,: quo nihil popularius est,: populare gratumque audientibus,.—
Of or belonging to the citizens (as opposed to the soldiery): quique rem agunt duelli, quique populare auspicium,; cf.; usually as subst.: popŭlāris, is, m., a citizen (post-class.): multa milia et popularium et militum,; : popularibus militibusque,; .—
Belonging to or fit for the common people; hence, common, coarse, mean, bad: sal. : pulli (apium),: popularia agere, to play coarse tricks, Laber. ap. .—Hence, adv.: pŏpŭlārĭter.
After the manner of the common people, i. e. commonly, coarsely, vulgarly, : loqui,: scriptus liber (opp. limatius),.—
In a popular manner, popularly, democratically: agere,: conciones seditiose ac populariter excitatae,: occidere quemlibet populariter,to win popularity,.

senses: a politician in the camp of the populares, opposed to the optimates

la:verb:populor.gloss: to lay waste, ravage or devastate, destroy or ruin
senses: to lay waste, ravage or devastate, destroy or ruin
la:verb:populor.html:
pŏpŭlor, ātus, 1. v. dep., and pŏpŭlo, āre, v. a.
1. populus; prop. to spread or pour out in a multitude over a region; hence, transf. to the result
,
to lay waste, ravage, devastate, desolate; to spoil, plunder, pillage (class.; syn.: vasto, vexo, diripio).
Lit.
Form populor: Romanus exercitus insulam integram urit, populatur, vastat, Naev. ap. : noctu populabatur agros,: Remorum agros,: arva ferro populatur et igni,; so, omnia igni ferroque populatus,: consules Aequos populantur, —
Form populo (in Cicero only in part. perf. pass.): patriam populavit meam, Pac. ap. : agrum populare coeperunt, Quadrig. : litora vestra Vi populat,: Penates,. —In pass.: urbem Romanam deūm irā morbo populari,; fin.: populata vexataque provincia,; cf.: Siculi nunc populati atque vexati,: arva Marte populata nostro,: populatis messibus,.—
Transf., in gen., to destroy, ruin, spoil (mostly poet. and in the active form), Plaut. ap. P.: populatque ingentem farris acervum Curculio,: capillos,: feris populandas tradere gentes,: populata tempora raptis Auribus,mutilated, deprived of,: populatum exspuit hamum,robbed of the bait,.—In a deponent form: quisque suum populatus iter,: iter,: formam populabitur aetas,: (ventus in Aetnā) Putria multivagis populatur flatibus antra,lays waste,.

Lit.: the ham of the knee, the hough (cf. suffrago): genua poplitesque et crura,: succisis feminibus poplitibusque,: succiso poplite,; cf. ; : elephas poplites intus flectit hominis modo,; .—

la:other:Popilius.html:
Popĭlĭus (Popill-), i, m., and Popi-lĭa (Popill-), ae, f.,
the name of a Roman gens. So esp.,
M. Popillius Laenas, a consul A. U.C. 395, .—
C. Popilius Laenas, the assassin of Cicero, ; .—
In fem.: Popilia,the wife of Q. Catulus,.— Hence,
Popĭlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Popilius, Popilian: gens,.

la:noun:populatio.html:
pŏpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f.
populor
,
a laying waste, ravaging, plundering, spoiling, devastation, etc. (not in Cic.).
Lit.: populationem effuse facere,.—In plur.: populationibus incursionibusque,: hostem rapinis, pabulationibus populationibusque prohibere,.—
Transf.
Concr., things plundered, plunder, booty: Veientes pleni populationum,.—
A ravaging, destroying done by animals: a populatione murium formicarumque frumenta defendere,; so, volucrum,.—
Trop., destruction, corruption, ruin (post-Aug.): morum,; of ruin through luxury, .

la:noun:popa.html:
pŏpa, ae, m.
A Roman inferior priest, a priest's assistant or minister, who brought the victim to the altar and felled it with an axe, ; ; ; . Alluding to the corpulence of such priests: popa venter,a fat paunch, glutton,.—*
In fem.: PHILEMA POPA DE INSVLA, perh. = she who sells animals for sacrifice, .
